evidence.label: Finite congruence lattices: characterization and undecidability
A negative solution to the finite lattice representation problem

headline: Some finite lattices are not the congruence lattice of any finite algebra, and no program can tell which.
scope: Finite nonempty lattices and finite algebras with any finite list of operations. Also full subgroup intervals in finite groups.
plain: An algebra's congruences are the groupings its operations respect, and they form a lattice. The finite lattice representation problem asks whether every finite lattice arises this way from a finite algebra. These papers claim the answer is no. They also claim no program can decide which finite lattices arise. A colored-graph test for which lattices arise has a Lean proof.
doesNot: This does not give the size of a counterexample, or a way to compute it.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Péter Pálfy and Pavel Pudlák, the link to subgroup intervals
scorecard.significanceWhy: It would settle a central open question of universal algebra, in the negative, and add an undecidability result.

explanation:
Take three objects, a, b and c. Sort them into groups. There are five ways: all apart, three ways to pair two of them, or all together. Ordered by merging, these five groupings form a small diagram. Mathematicians call such a diagram a lattice: any two of its points have a least point above both and a greatest point below both.

Now add a rule that moves a to b, b to c, and c to a. Call a grouping a congruence if the rule respects it. Objects in one group must land in one group. Pairing a with b now fails, because the rule then pairs b with c. Only two groupings survive: all apart and all together. A finite algebra is a finite set with finitely many such rules. Its congruences, ordered by merging, always form a lattice. Different rules give different lattices.

The finite lattice representation problem runs the other way. Pick any finite lattice. Is there a finite algebra whose congruences form exactly that lattice, with nothing extra? The rules may be anything at all, and as many as needed.

Grätzer and Schmidt showed in 1963 that every lattice of a broad kind is the congruence lattice of some algebra[1]. That algebra need not be finite[2]. In 1980, Pálfy and Pudlák tied the finite question to finite groups. Every finite lattice has a finite algebra exactly when every finite lattice is an interval in the subgroup lattice of a finite group[3]. That interval is the set of subgroups between two fixed ones. Many lattices were known to work. Every finite lattice of width at most two does[4]. Among lattices with at most seven elements, only one possible exception was left, and the paper handles it[5].

The two papers claim the answer is no. One claims there is a finite lattice that no finite algebra of any kind realizes[6]. The other claims something stronger. No computer program can take a lattice's table and always decide whether a finite algebra realizes it[7]. If every lattice worked, the program that always says yes would decide it. So the stronger claim also gives the negative answer[11]. The same undecidability is claimed for subgroup intervals in finite groups[8]. There is a smallest counterexample, with more than seven elements[9]. Its description uses a Busy Beaver number, so its actual size is not computed[12].

The single obstacle is that nothing about a hypothetical algebra is bounded. Every lattice in the argument is finite. But a group realizing it could have any order, any rank and any field size[13]. The paper builds lattices whose shapes force long chains of simple subgroups inside any such group. It then needs a bound on those chains that holds for every finite group at once[14]. The classification of finite simple groups, a large body of earlier work, supplies the key inputs[15].

There is also a positive tool. The paper turns a lattice into a question about finite colored graphs. A lattice is realizable exactly when a suitable colored graph exists[10]. Searching through graphs finds every yes answer. What fails is a stopping rule for the no answers[16].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has a formal proof of the colored-graph criterion. That covers the equivalence between realizability and the graph test. The undecidability results, the subgroup-interval result and the counterexample lie outside that check. They rest on long arguments using the classification of finite simple groups. No specialist review of either paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds. Only the colored-graph criterion has a Lean proof; the negative answer and undecidability rest on long arguments using the classification of finite simple groups. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: An ordered set where any two elements have a least element above both and a greatest element below both.
A finite nonempty set with a finite list of operations, each taking a fixed number of inputs.
A grouping of an algebra's elements that its operations respect: grouped inputs give grouped outputs.
All subgroups of a group lying between two fixed subgroups, ordered by inclusion.
No computer program can answer every instance of the question correctly and always stop.
A specific whole number defined from small computer programs; it exists, but no general method computes such numbers.
